# Rendering Pipelines and Extensions


## Overview
This family encompasses extensions to the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline that modify the attribute representation, compositing logic, or execution framework to support specific domains such as volume visualization, physically-based rendering, or cross-platform compilation . Unlike standard 3DGS which uses view-dependent color and opacity for emissive/absorptive splatting, these methods decouple geometry from appearance or replace the rasterization backend to enable features like dynamic relighting, scalar field transfer functions, or portable execution .

## Shared principles
All extensions retain the core 3D Gaussian primitive representation: a set of $M$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian kernels $\mathcal{G} = \{G_i\}_{i=1}^M$ [G]. Each kernel is defined by:
*   $\mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$: Position (mean) [G].
*   $\mathbf{R}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$: Rotation matrix [G].
*   $\mathbf{S}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$: Scale matrix [G].
*   The covariance matrix is $\mathbf{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{R}_i \mathbf{S}_i \mathbf{S}_i^\top \mathbf{R}_i^\top$ [G].

The rendering pipeline's geometric projection remains consistent for ray-based methods: 3D Gaussians are transformed into ray space, and the projected 2D covariance $\mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}_i$ is computed using the Jacobian $J$ of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part $W$ of the extrinsic matrix:
$$ \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}_i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}_i W^T J^T $$
[G].

However, the attribute representation and loss functions diverge significantly from the standard RGB opacity/color model [G]. Standard 3DGS uses view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}_i(\mathbf{d})$ [G]. In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors [G].

## Subtopics

### [Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering](2063-gaussian-splatting-volume-rendering.md)
A differentiable rendering technique that synthesizes images by projecting 3D Gaussian distributions onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them. It solves the problem of high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis by replacing traditional triangle meshes with explicit, optimizable Gaussian primitives. It sets itself apart from standard ray marching by avoiding iterative sampling, instead using a tile-based rasterization strategy for parallelization. It focuses on the efficient rasterization and compositing of emissive/absorptive Gaussians.

### [Rendering and Lighting Pipelines](4135-rendering-and-lighting-pipelines.md)
Extends the standard rasterization pipeline to support advanced transparency handling, volumetric lighting, and physically-based inverse rendering. While standard 3DGS uses order-dependent alpha blending, these methods introduce order-independent transparency, ray-marched volume occlusion, and material decomposition to solve artifacts like popping and lack of shadows.

### [Volume Encoding Gaussians](6093-volume-encoding-gaussians.md)
Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume data visualization by removing per-Gaussian color and opacity attributes, training only scalar values to enable interactive transfer function application post-training. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering by decoupling the volumetric density representation from the visual appearance, allowing dynamic remapping of scalar fields to color and opacity without retraining.

### [BRDF and Relighting Extensions](6227-brdf-and-relighting-extensions.md)
Extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling material properties from geometry and lighting, enabling physically-based rendering (PBR) and dynamic relighting. Unlike standard splatting which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics coefficients via an emission-absorption model, these methods store per-Gaussian BRDF parameters (e.g., albedo, roughness, metalness) and evaluate them against arbitrary light sources. This allows for accurate specular reflections and shadow casting.

### [XPR Rendering Pipeline](17626-xpr-rendering-pipeline.md)
A framework for point-based differentiable rendering that decouples method-specific logic from the shared rendering pipeline. It separates the core rendering mechanics—parallelization, data layout, tiling, and differentiation—from the primitive evaluation logic, enabling portable execution across GPUs, TPUs, and CPUs via the XLA compiler. Unlike traditional CUDA implementations, XPR exposes a four-function interface that captures only the method-specific math.

## Background
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 . Subsequent extensions emerged to address limitations in lighting (BRDF), volume visualization (scalar encoding), and deployment portability (XPR) .
